questions.q: What is inheritance defined as in biology?
a: The transmission of genetic information from generation to generation
The random mutation of DNA sequences
The physical growth of an organism from a seed
The breakdown of food in the digestive tract

questions.q: What is a chromosome?
a: A protein that digests food
A thread-like structure of DNA, made up of a string of genes, found in the nucleus of cells
A type of plant hormone
An organelle responsible for respiration

questions.q: What is a gene defined as?
a: An entire human chromosome
A complete set of proteins in a cell
A length of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A carbohydrate molecule stored in the liver

questions.q: What is an allele?
a: A physical trait like eye color
An extra chromosome in a cell
A cellular organelle
An alternative form of a gene

questions.q: What does the term 'haploid' mean?
a: Having a nucleus containing a single set of unpaired chromosomes (e.g., in gametes, n = 23 in humans)
Having two complete sets of chromosomes
Having no chromosomes
Having chromosomes made of RNA only

questions.q: What does the term 'diploid' mean?
a: Having half the normal number of chromosomes
Having a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes (e.g., in body somatic cells, 2n = 46 in humans)
Having chromosomes arranged in triplets
Having abnormal mutated genes

questions.q: What is mitosis defined as?
a: A type of cell division that produces genetically different haploid gametes
The fusion of two nuclei during fertilization
A nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells in which the chromosome number is maintained (diploid to diploid)
The process of protein synthesis

questions.q: What is meiosis defined as?
a: Division of bacterial cells by binary fission
The repair of broken skin cells
Growth of plant stems toward light
A reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid, resulting in genetically different gametes

questions.q: What is genotype defined as?
a: The genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles it possesses (e.g., Bb or homozygous)
The physical observable appearance of an organism
The environmental impact on traits
The number of chromosomes in a cell

questions.q: What is phenotype defined as?
a: The sequence of nitrogenous bases in DNA
The observable features or characteristics of an organism resulting from its genotype interacting with the environment
The recessive alleles hidden in carriers
The total weight of an organism

questions.q: What is a dominant allele?
a: An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present
An allele that is destroyed by mutations
An allele that is expressed if it is present in either single or double dose (heterozygous or homozygous)
An allele found only on the Y chromosome

questions.q: What is a recessive allele?
a: An allele that always masks dominant traits
An allele that is found exclusively in plant cells
An allele that causes instant cell death
An allele that is only expressed when the dominant allele is absent (i.e., in homozygous recessive condition, e.g., bb)

questions.q: What does 'homozygous' mean?
a: Having two identical alleles of a particular gene (e.g., BB or bb)
Having two different alleles of a gene (e.g., Bb)
Having no alleles for a trait
Having chromosomes of unequal length

questions.q: What does 'heterozygous' mean?
a: Having two identical recessive alleles
Having two different alleles of a particular gene (e.g., Bb)
Having multiple nuclei in a cell
Having missing genes on a chromosome

questions.q: In humans, what are the sex chromosomes for a normal biological female?
a: XY
OY
XX
XXY

questions.q: In humans, what are the sex chromosomes for a normal biological male?
a: XX
YY
XO
XY

questions.q: What is a mutation defined as?
a: A genetic change in the base sequence of DNA or chromosome number, which is the sole source of new alleles
The normal duplication of cells during mitosis
The inheritance of parental traits unchanged
The fusion of male and female gametes

questions.q: Which of the following environmental factors can increase the rate of gene mutations (mutagens)?
a: Pure distilled water and oxygen
Ionizing radiation (e.g., X-rays, ultraviolet radiation) and chemical mutagens (e.g., tobacco tar chemicals)
Excess dietary protein and sleep
Moderate aerobic exercise

questions.q: What is sickle cell anemia an example of?
a: A bacterial infection spread by mosquitoes
A nutritional deficiency disease caused by lack of iron
An inherited genetic disease caused by a mutation in the hemoglobin gene, leading to abnormal sickle-shaped red blood cells
A viral respiratory condition

questions.q: Why are people who are heterozygous for the sickle cell allele (carriers, Hb^A Hb^S) at an evolutionary advantage in regions where malaria is common?
a: They are immune to all bacterial infections
They possess extra red blood cells
They can run faster in high altitudes
The malaria parasite cannot reproduce successfully inside their slightly altered sickle-shaped red blood cells, conferring resistance to malaria

questions.q: What is continuous variation?
a: Variation where characteristics fall into a distinct range of measurable values with many intermediate forms controlled by multiple genes and environmental influence (e.g., human height or skin color)
Variation where individuals belong to distinct, non-overlapping categories (e.g., blood groups A, B, AB, O)
Variation caused exclusively by single gene mutations
Variation that never changes over time

questions.q: What is discontinuous variation?
a: Variation showing a continuous bell curve of measurements
Variation where features fall into distinct, discrete categories with no intermediates, usually controlled by a single gene (e.g., blood groups or earlobe attachment)
Variation caused entirely by diet and exercise
Variation that is identical across different species

questions.q: What is natural selection defined as?
a: The artificial breeding of dogs by humans for desirable traits
The random disappearance of species over time
The process by which better-adapted organisms are more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on their advantageous alleles to their offspring
The inheritance of acquired physical skills

questions.q: What is selective breeding (artificial selection) by humans?
a: Natural adaptation of animals to harsh weather without human interference
The random mutation of crops in the wild
The extinction of weak animal species
The process by which humans breed animals or plants with desirable characteristics to produce offspring with those traits

questions.q: What is evolution defined as in biological science?
a: The change in adaptive features of a population over time through natural selection
The rapid growth of an individual during its lifetime
The division of cells by mitosis
The stable maintenance of species without any genetic changes

questions.q: Which scientist is most famously associated with developing the theory of evolution by natural selection alongside Alfred Russel Wallace?
a: Gregor Mendel
Charles Darwin
Louis Pasteur
Robert Hooke

questions.q: What role do antibiotic-resistant bacteria ('superbugs') play in demonstrating natural selection?
a: They prove that bacteria can perform photosynthesis
They show how human medicines are always 100 percent effective
They demonstrate how random mutations and the selective pressure of antibiotics allow resistant bacterial strains to survive, reproduce, and take over the population
They show that bacteria have no DNA

questions.q: What is a pedigree chart used for in genetics?
a: To map out the weather patterns affecting crop growth
To measure the exact weight of chromosomes
To calculate plant transpiration rates
To trace the inheritance of specific genetic traits or disorders through generations of a family

questions.q: What is the expected phenotypic ratio in the offspring of a cross between two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) for a simple dominant/recessive trait?
a: 3 dominant to 1 recessive (75 percent dominant, 25 percent recessive)
100 percent heterozygous
1 dominant to 1 recessive
All recessive

questions.q: What is an allele that is masked in a heterozygous individual called?
a: Codominant
Recessive
Dominant
Mutated

questions.q: What is codominance?
a: When one allele completely masks another
When genes are located on the Y chromosome only
A situation in which both alleles in a heterozygous organism are expressed fully in the phenotype (e.g., AB blood group)
When mutations occur spontaneously

questions.q: Which of the following human characteristics is an example of discontinuous variation?
a: Height
Body mass
Foot length
ABO blood group

questions.q: What is adaptation defined as in the context of evolution and natural selection?
a: The process, resulting from natural selection, by which populations become more suited to their environment over generations
The conscious choice of an animal to change its color
The artificial modification of genes in a laboratory
The physical injury of an organism during its life

questions.q: Why is genetic variation within a species population important for survival?
a: It ensures all individuals are identical
It provides a wider range of traits so that if the environment changes or a new disease strikes, some individuals are more likely to possess advantageous alleles and survive
It prevents mutations from occurring
It stops competition between organisms

questions.q: What is the role of messenger RNA (mRNA) in protein synthesis?
a: To store permanent genetic master codes in the cell center
To physically build bones
To carry a transcribed copy of the genetic code from the DNA in the nucleus to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm
To break down glucose into energy

questions.q: Who is historically known as the 'father of genetics' for his breeding experiments with pea plants?
a: Charles Darwin
James Watson
Francis Crick
Gregor Mendel
